reviews.text: "The Grand Budapest Hotel is Wes Anderson’s greatest cinematic achievement yet, bursting with bold visuals and dynamic storytelling."
reviews.author: Jack Walters

reviews.text: “The Grand Budapest Hotel” may be an audiovisual feast, but what makes it an artistic marvel is that its dynamic style enhances the narrative’s focus on its primary characters through different decades.
reviews.author: Ankit Ojha

reviews.text: It’s not hard to see why The Grand Budapest Hotel has gleaned such love over the past seven years. It is a perfect encapsulation of the best of Anderson’s works, with its fast-paced dialogue and candy coloured visual palette
reviews.author: Christopher Connor

reviews.text: Perhaps the filmmaker’s most culturally relevant works, The Grand Budapest Hotel saw Anderson flex his production design chops as hard as he ever had.
reviews.author: Cory Woodroof

reviews.text: ...a variety of post-production work is highlighted, from color correction of the typically fastidiously coordinated hotel to the mechanics of the dizzying climactic downhill mountain chase...
reviews.author: Vadim Rizov

reviews.text: Wes Anderson blends his trademark fanciness with a more rompish style of humour than usual.
reviews.author: Edward Porter

reviews.text: It definitely comes more into focus the more times you see it.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: Even from a single viewing, an audience knows they have seen what surely must be one of Anderson's best works to date.
reviews.author: Brian Eggert

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's bright, meticulous style reaches its most complete expression in this painfully poignant period comedy.
reviews.author: Calum Baker

reviews.text: It's is an adventure, a murder mystery, an old-world tale, a storybook fable, and a sinister conspiracy. But under the cake-frosting colors and period gilt is a bittersweet story about a way of life hanging on in a world modernizing and passing it by...
reviews.author: Sean Axmaker

reviews.text: Something this exciting to look at and listen to, something this light and entertaining, shouldn’t leave a viewer so unsatisfied.
reviews.author: Dan Bayer

reviews.text: It is a gorgeous movie; both comedic as well as emotional until the very last moment. Another great film by Anderson.
reviews.author: Therese Lacson

reviews.text: This is Wes at his most over-the-top and accessible - somehow simultaneously.
reviews.author: Sophie Charara

reviews.text: Amongst the whole spread of frequent Anderson collaborators, it is Ralph Fiennes, in the spotlight, who makes the most of every second he has on-screen. The end result is a flurry of cotton candy feelings.
reviews.author: Kanishk Devgan

reviews.text: Wes Anderson finds a balance between his highly stylized artistic vision, story and heart.
reviews.author: Richard Crouse

reviews.text: No one crafts characters, worlds, and stories quite like Wes Anderson.
reviews.author: Mike Massie

reviews.text: The film's wholly fictionalized history and its meticulously composed imagery overlay the darkest thematic innards the filmmaker has yet composed, near-seamlessly melding its war-torn heart with a Mendl's sugary coating.
reviews.author: Jordan M. Smith

reviews.text: It is a film best experienced with a heart and mind fully open.
reviews.author: Richard Propes

reviews.text: There's a tantalising darkness just beneath the surface of Anderson's trademark whacky whimsy in his latest offering, The Grand Budapest Hotel, making it one of the year's most unforgettable films
reviews.author: Stephen A. Russell

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's newest film, The Grand Budapest Hotel, is a stylish, fantastical film, sometimes comic and sometimes tragic in its re-imagining...
reviews.author: Joanne Laurier

reviews.text: At 45 the Wes Anderson metaphor reaches its peak and is still more polymorphic than ever. 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' is another eccentricity of its world, where tragicomedy wraps itself of dreams without the need to wake up. [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Yasser Medina

reviews.text: "Times have changed." It's an elemental Wes Anderson lament...
reviews.author: Adam Kempenaar

reviews.text: From Ralph Fiennes' dapper strut to Willem Dafoe's pointy teeth, every detail feels just right in the best film of Wes Anderson's career.
reviews.author: Matt Brunson

reviews.text: The desire to show fantastic worlds and tell stories in the face of the inevitable march of time and destructive forces is at the core of the film. Anderson's films are beginning to show the soul beneath the exactitude.
reviews.author: Jim Ross

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is a fast-paced beautiful spectacle that never ceases to amuse you.
reviews.author: Shikhar Verma

reviews.text: Magnificent and magical, once you check-in, you'll never want to check-out.
reviews.author: Debbie Lynn Elias

reviews.text: To alter a phrase from Batman, who won't mind because he's not real, The Grand Budapest Hotel is the movie audiences deserve and the one Anderson needed.
reviews.author: Ryan Syrek

reviews.text: Those of you who worship at the auteur altar of the director, who have long embraced his fastidious, meticulous style of studied nostalgia and to-the-inch symmetrical specificity, need no prodding.
reviews.author: Leslie Combemale

reviews.text: Anderson's particular aesthetic can sometimes serve to keep the audience at arm's length, but here it achieves something deeply beautiful, even warm and inviting.
reviews.author: Mattie Lucas

reviews.text: What the film amounts to is nothing more than a well-done and admirable piece of fluff.
reviews.author: C.J. Prince

reviews.text: The sometimes erratic tone and plot machinations mean it may not be perfect, but ignore your reservations and check in to The Grand Budapest Hotel.
reviews.author: Chris Davies

reviews.text: A cat and mouse chase with a lot of humor and whimsey.
reviews.author: Rachel Wagner

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is immense fun and, as far as Anderson's oeuvre is concerned, unquestionably the rarest of fillet steak.
reviews.author: Ben Nicholson

reviews.text: It is certainly a magical and childlike way of storytelling, even if the content is a little more adult.
reviews.author: Paula Fleri-Soler

reviews.text: This might just be Wes Anderson's best film; it's certainly his most thrilling. The cult director has bolstered the whimsical humor with a raucous crime caper and it's a riot.
reviews.author: Nico Hines

reviews.text: It all seems kind of silly and trivial, but under Anderson's screenplay -- inspired by the works of Stefan Zweig -- it's tied together with a bit of a melancholy sweetness that gives it some unexpected heart.
reviews.author: Micheal Compton

reviews.text: I didn't find it amusing, and while I can appreciate the creativity, it's an hour and 40 minutes I wish I could take back.
reviews.author: Amanda Greever

reviews.text: The conceit of having the film refracted through four stories-within-stories beautifully thematises the idea of nostalgia and storytelling as part of our balm of remembrance.
reviews.author: PJ Nabarro

reviews.text: I wouldn't describe it as a film that will have a profound impact on your psyche. It is however a visually delightful, beautifully acted tale.
reviews.author: Debbie Baldwin

reviews.text: Fans of the director will not be disappointed, almost expecting the bit of meandering that occurs in the middle that is immediately forgiven in the context of the whole.
reviews.author: Sarah Gopaul

reviews.text: Like a beautiful stacking petruschka doll - open up another and another of its layers until you reach an empty center.
reviews.author: Pat Padua

reviews.text: The movie is so lush with detail that only a big screen can do it justice.
reviews.author: Marcianne Miller

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's overly considered cinematic world has never felt so expansive, enveloping, and infectiously fun.
reviews.author: Mark Keizer

reviews.text: With an absolute stellar cast and Adrien Brody's moustache deserving its own line in the credits this film is about as sweet as some Mendl's confectionary. Five Stars.
reviews.author: Chloe Leeson

reviews.text: Handsome, opulent and cunningly devised.
reviews.author: Joseph Walsh

reviews.text: [Wes Anderson has[ made his most Wes Anderson-ian film yet, "The Grand Budapest Hotel," and it is utterly glorious.
reviews.author: Asia Frey

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is such an ode to the old world, and to those who have immortalized it in words and pictures.
reviews.author: Oggs Cruz

reviews.text: The theme seems to be a kind of late-Edwardian Euro whimsy along Wodehousian lines... except that Wodehouse was really funny, and Anderson really isn't.
reviews.author: Camilla Long

reviews.text: Whether you call this an exaggeratedly tall tale or simply a good old shaggy dog story, its ultimate meaning matters less than its maker's lavish deployment of a whimsy so powerful it could almost be thermonuclear.
reviews.author: Lynden Barber

reviews.text: Discerning travellers and Wes Anderson fans will luxuriate in the glorious Mittel-European kitsch of one of the director's funniest and most exquisitely designed movies in years.
reviews.author: Kate Muir

reviews.text: Anderson proposes a kind of chivalric novel with nineteenth century airs from a wonderful staging... [Full review in Spanish]
reviews.author: Hugo Hernández Valdivia

reviews.text: This whimsical tale oozes charm while brisk editing lets you enjoy - but not be overwhelmed by - cakes like mountains and mountains like cakes, chandeliers, perfumed men and Persian pussies.
reviews.author: Srijana Mitra Das

reviews.text: It's the most emotionally satisfying Anderson film since Rushmore, and its quirks and whimsies are kept right on the edge of indulgence without ever actually tipping over.
reviews.author: Sarah Marrs

reviews.text: [Wes Anderson's] nostalgia, like his set design, is so contrived that I don't believe he really believes in it as anything other than a visual style. The Grand Budapest Hotel is a perfect miniature world, but it left me cold.
reviews.author: Anwen Crawford

reviews.text: As usual, it's beautifully set-designed, impeccably scored and acted with all the emotion of Hannibal Lecter on a bender.
reviews.author: Tara Thorne

reviews.text: It's one to lose yourself in.
reviews.author: Russell Baillie

reviews.text: There's a slightly darker edge to The Grand Budapest Hotel than Anderson's previous efforts.
reviews.author: Sonny Bunch

reviews.text: In The Grand Budapest Hotel we can sense both a progression and summarizing of the entire Wes Anderson canon.
reviews.author: Nick Newman

reviews.text: Just plain fun, full of the filmmaker's signature flourishes and curlicues, worked out with skill and finesse.
reviews.author: Jason Bailey

reviews.text: Wes Anderson makes great kid movies. He had me at 'Moonrise Kingdom' and 'Fantastic Mr. Fox.' Grown-up movie-wise, Wes's weird world makes this reviewer weary.
reviews.author: Mark Jackson

reviews.text: For anyone who has long suspected Wes Anderson of being a master technician in search of his heart, The Grand Budapest Hotel joyfully announces that the quest is over.
reviews.author: Bill Newcott

reviews.text: Whimsical, frothy fun doesn't go down any easier than this, let alone with a performance as marvelous as Fiennes'.
reviews.author: J. Olson

reviews.text: I can't claim Anderson doesn't have a certain power as a filmmaker. But after watching The Grand Budapest Hotel, it seems clear he doesn't use his power for good.
reviews.author: Eileen Jones

reviews.text: "The Grand Budapest Hotel" is not a callous work, but it's about packing painful experience in storage.
reviews.author: Rob Gonsalves

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's superb eye for visual storytelling comes to a head with this luscious murder mystery that starts out in an exclusive luxury hotel and thrills the audience throughout Europe.
reviews.author: Wesley Lovell

reviews.text: A grownup storybook of a movie spun out of candy-colored nonsense that challenges you to embrace its falseness and deny its romance.
reviews.author: MaryAnn Johanson

reviews.text: Ralph Fiennes holds civilization together with little more than his impeccable manners and mustache in Wes Anderson's absurdist dollhouse of a tragicomedy.
reviews.author: Chris Barsanti

reviews.text: Many Wes Anderson films have been intricately laced together, the ingredients blending just so. But nothing matches this perfectly layered concoction, wrapped up in an impeccable confectioner's bow.
reviews.author: Kimberly Gadette

reviews.text: In theory, we all should know that stepping into a theater automatically makes what we are about to see a story within a story - but director Wes Anderson delights in showing us the artifice
reviews.author: Luke Y. Thompson

reviews.text: "The Grand Budapest Hotel" is not his grandest work yet, but it is one worth an extended stay.
reviews.author: Kate Erbland

reviews.text: With apologies to Willy Wonka and his wallpaper-licking visitors, the titular Alpine resort is the most edible-looking lodge in cinema: a multitiered, pink-frosted castle designed to endure as an ambrosial memory.
reviews.author: Aaron Mesh

reviews.text: Those like myself who admire auteur-driven filmmaking can celebrate with the release of "The Grand Budapest Hotel," the best movie of 2014 at this early stage, and perhaps likely to remain so for some time to come.
reviews.author: Michael Smith

reviews.text: Once again, Anderson has managed to make an affecting, funny movie; it may be more melancholy than most, but bittersweet love is love nonetheless, and The Grand Budapest Hotel is worth visiting multiple times.
reviews.author: Alex Doenau

reviews.text: Anderson's admirers will love it, while those who resist his quirky mix of deadpan precision and manic disorder must grant that it fits the story he tells here.
reviews.author: Jim Lane

reviews.text: The mannered, madcap proceedings are often delightful, occasionally silly, and here and there, gruesome and/or heartbreaking.
reviews.author: Matthew Lickona

reviews.text: The result is as offbeat as any of Anderson's films, but more heartfelt than most.
reviews.author: Sean P. Means

reviews.text: The lingering impact of the movie is slighter than it hopes to be, a pastiche full of sound and whimsy, signifying nothing.
reviews.author: Genevieve Valentine

reviews.text: There's more creativity and inventiveness on display here than in the rest of last weekend's top 10 box-office draws combined.
reviews.author: Christopher Lawrence

reviews.text: No matter who you are, this movie will charm your dandy pants off and then some.
reviews.author: Michael Arbeiter

reviews.text: "The Grand Budapest Hotel" is Anderson's finest attempt at film whimsy. He's created a movie that is as visually stunning as it is smartly written.
reviews.author: Rick Bentley

reviews.text: Like most of Anderson's films -- and Gustave himself -- the film is rather pleased with itself, but its exuberant humour and pacy plot keep it accessible while Fiennes delivers his funniest role ever.
reviews.author: David Edwards

reviews.text: While The Grand Budapest Hotel is delightfully good fun, it's the moments of pathos and black humour that reveal the scope of its achievements.
reviews.author: Luke Buckmaster

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel isn't just a fantastic argument for Anderson as artist -- it's probably the best formally interesting movie that's also meaningful in years.
reviews.author: Jackson Cuidon

reviews.text: We have another minor masterpiece to add to [Anderson's] growing pile of textiles.
reviews.author: Piers Marchant

reviews.text: People tend to either love or hate Anderson's direction. I don't think this film will change anyone's mind, but if you do do enjoy his work, I think that you'll really enjoy this one.
reviews.author: Scott Nash

reviews.text: This is a visually stunning film, but above all it's a hugely enjoyable one.
reviews.author: David Stratton

reviews.text: I like Anderson when he's making movies about childhood -- "Rushmore," or "Fantastic Mr. Fox" -- but when he ventures into the realm of adulthood, he seems out of his jurisdiction.
reviews.author: Gary Thompson

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's latest opus, The Grand Budapest Hotel, is bloody bonkers and simply splendid.
reviews.author: Bruce Kirkland

reviews.text: Grand isn't good enough a word for this Budapest Hotel. Great is more like it.
reviews.author: Richard Corliss

reviews.text: Anderson's films are too precious for some, but for those of us willing to lose ourselves in them, they're a delight. "The Grand Budapest Hotel" is no different, except that he has added a hint of gravitas to the mix, improving the recipe.
reviews.author: Bill Goodykoontz

reviews.text: "The Grand Budapest Hotel" is about far more than just a ridiculous play of manners of a bygone age. It is truly a celebration of narration and of storytelling.
reviews.author: Anders Wright

reviews.text: While the enigmatic details and nuances are the very treasures and treats being gifted, they are mere trinkets when not combined with the style and imagery that Anderson has forged from his creative spirit.
reviews.author: Jordan Hiller

reviews.text: A joy and sight to behold from beginning to end, The Grand Budapest Hotel is pure filmmaking delight. It's one of 2014's best.
reviews.author: Bill Clark

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is funny and offbeat, zips along at a pleasing pace, and in M. Gustave has a truly memorable leading character.
reviews.author: Martin Roberts

reviews.text: For his fans this tribute to a bygone era and in fact a bygone world is a brilliant watch, one of the most thoughtful of Anderson's films even amongst the grandiose escapism.
reviews.author: Hannah Strong

reviews.text: What is remarkable is that instead of overcooking this film, the big names add value to a remarkably inventive and wholeheartedly fun, cinema-going experience.
reviews.author: Graham Young

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel may be Wes Anderson's most finely-crafted film to date, and is one that even the filmmaker's detractors should be able to appreciate.
reviews.author: Austin Trunick

reviews.text: Wes Anderson mais Wes Anderson do que nunca.
reviews.author: Pablo Villaça

reviews.text: Hundreds of precious little moments but not much beyond extravagant artifice to sink your teeth into.
reviews.author: Bruce Bennett

reviews.text: The ultimate reason why [it] feels fresh and vibrant [is because] it harkens so far back in movie history to find its inspiration that it proves the old "everything old is new again" maxim is true.
reviews.author: Richard Knight

reviews.text: A beautiful dream that helps us deal with the slings and arrows of our banal real world with a little more pluck.
reviews.author: Rob Vaux

reviews.text: Anderson and his crew build an impeccable, elaborate world that is opulent and breathtaking, yet somewhat silly.
reviews.author: Jeffrey M. Anderson

reviews.text: The movie may suffer from some of its quick-and-done plotting, but its quality of humor, spectacle, and acting is all top notch.
reviews.author: Jack Giroux

reviews.text: Anderson's film looks good enough to eat; swallowing it is another matter.
reviews.author: Melissa Anderson

reviews.text: This wacky screwball comedy, loosely based on stories by Stefan Zweig, has a plot so labyrinthine and frantic it is hardly worth following, except for the fantastic sets and appealing central characters played by Ralph Fiennes and Tony Revolori.
reviews.author: Robert Roten

reviews.text: An argument could be made that this is Wes Anderson's best film.
reviews.author: Matt Neal

reviews.text: Anderson's sights are like scenes from a storybook, and the actors move and speak with a clockwork cadence that adds to the sense of comedic orchestration.
reviews.author: Neil Pond

reviews.text: Watching Wes Anderson quietly and unsentimentally make Zero the hero of The Grand Budapest Hotel should win over some of the director's detractors.
reviews.author: John P. McCarthy

reviews.text: It is a film that maintains its illusion with grace-and ruefully unmasks that illusion every bit as gracefully.
reviews.author: Jonathan Romney

reviews.text: Fans of director Wes Anderson, here's what you've been waiting for since you saw 'Moonrise Kingdom.' 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' is another comedy with quirky characters and oddball encounters.
reviews.author: Linda Cook

reviews.text: A typically witless comedy from Wes Anderson that has about as much to do with Stefan Zweig as it does with WWII and Nazism, the disasters that led to Zweig's suicide in 1942. A total travesty.
reviews.author: Louis Proyect

reviews.text: Runs in the vein of Anderson's more exotic pictures (think 'The Life Aquatic' and 'The Darjeeling Limited').
reviews.author: Brad Keefe

reviews.text: Any single frame qualifies for wall space in a cinematic museum as the players ingeniously apply their emotive elasticity to fit the Anderson universe.
reviews.author: Jules Brenner

reviews.text: Eloquent, offbeat and charming, The Grand Budapest Hotel is Anderson's most accomplished film to date.
reviews.author: Tom Glasson

reviews.text: Fiennes is magnificent, his droll wit and a "keep calm and carry on" delivery occasionally peppered with highlights of profanity and fire. Comedic timing perfection.
reviews.author: Tim Martain

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's The Grand Budapest Hotel is a work of visceral, madcap comedic genius.
reviews.author: Blake Howard

reviews.text: Another visually scrumptious cinematic doily from America's master of over-designed whimsy, Wes Anderson, and this one is measurably better than many of his previous efforts in that there's something resembling a plot at the heart of it.
reviews.author: Jim Schembri

reviews.text: Filled with fully fleshed out characters, amazing dialogue and a look that is right out of the 1940s, the film travels smoothly on the shoulders of Ralph Fiennes.
reviews.author: Michael A. Smith

reviews.text: A fairytale for adults, this is Anderson's über-film thus far, utilising the entire breadth and astonishing depth of his imagination to bear exquisite humour and life in every single, immaculately composed shot.
reviews.author: CJ Johnson

reviews.text: Anderson's focus on oddball humor, audaciously eloquent dialogue, and cartoonish absurdity remains central and doesn't get derailed by the overly forced attempts at familial pathos that have marred some of his other films
reviews.author: James Kendrick

reviews.text: swallowed whole by the grey beast solipsism.
reviews.author: Walter Chaw

reviews.text: It's satisfying to see this level of craftsmanship applied to a film that is often so silly it's a pure delight to watch.
reviews.author: Steve Newall

reviews.text: From every angle, The Grand Budapest Hotel delivers so much to love, laugh along with, and lean forward for a better look at.
reviews.author: Leigh Paatsch

reviews.text: This is full of the elements you expect to find in a Wes Anderson film. There are lovingly composed tableaus - each a marvel of production design - immaculately designed uniforms for both soldiers and hotel bellboys and a sighting of Bill Murray.
reviews.author: Craig Mathieson

reviews.text: This is about as fun as movie-going gets. Fans of Anderson's work should love it; those who've disliked the artifice and nostalgia of his earlier films will find those elements put to more entertaining use here.
reviews.author: Anthony Morris

reviews.text: Anderson is at the middle of point of his life, considering the uncertainty of the world.
reviews.author: Damien Straker

reviews.text: Often lazily and unfairly accused of crafting works that trump style over substance, Anderson's painstaking attention to detail here beautifully serves the story.
reviews.author: Cara Nash

reviews.text: It's an eloquent, observant and mature comedy about the decay of an era.
reviews.author: Dennis Schwartz

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is as inventive and immaculately orchestrated a cinematic universe as I've ever seen.
reviews.author: Simon Miraudo

reviews.text: It is beautifully designed, visually ravishing and symmetrical to the nth degree. And it is full of frantic chaos, with a Lord of Misrule at its centre played with effortless comic brilliance by Ralph Fiennes.
reviews.author: Philippa Hawker

reviews.text: The success of Anderson's admirable ambition is to have elevated anachronism, pastiche, personal passions and larger cultural memory to a heady froth, but one that also knows the butt-end of a rifle.
reviews.author: Ray Pride

reviews.text: In addition to being a character-driven caper, beautifully designed, it's also an excellent tribute to the act of yearning for a better world.
reviews.author: Jonathan Kiefer

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is another feather in the cap of this wonderful director. It's quaint, charming and poignant.
reviews.author: Matthew Toomey

reviews.text: Every single frame ... is mesmerising, fascinating, surprising, fabulous, a stunning construct of colours and textures, the surreal and the visceral
reviews.author: Andrew L. Urban

reviews.text: Brilliantly conceived and executed ... dry, droll and delightful. It's a treasure trove of wonders - visually and emotionally - with its stylised, colourful production design
reviews.author: Louise Keller

reviews.text: With his latest, the time has arrived to stop thinking of Anderson's movies as great to look at and start thinking of them simply as great.
reviews.author: Rick Kisonak

reviews.text: Farcical pleasures are plentiful in Wes Anderson's The Grand Budapest Hotel, set in an eastern European republic steeped in Marxism. Groucho, not Karl.
reviews.author: Steve Persall

reviews.text: Funny, if not gut-busting, and well-executed, if not a masterpiece.
reviews.author: Eric D. Snider

reviews.text: The film that Wes Anderson was born for.
reviews.author: Tim Brayton

reviews.text: Anderson's script is sharp and funny, and never bashful about pausing the laughs for such melancholic reflections, mostly to grieve the loss of a time and place, and occasionally the people.
reviews.author: Kirk Baird

reviews.text: Anderson serves his guests meticulously assembled fun in "The Grand Budapest Hotel."
reviews.author: John Wirt

reviews.text: A stylistic and thematic progression, it's Anderson's most complex, nuanced effort, and his bawdiest, perhaps funniest, screenplay yet. It may be his masterpiece.
reviews.author: John Serba

reviews.text: Can you make a successful comedy entirely out of eccentric, marginally related episodes? The Grand Budapest Hotel proves it's possible, if you're Wes Anderson.
reviews.author: Lawrence Toppman

reviews.text: Dreams die gentle deaths as characters adjust and adapt, and try to find humanity in a world in which the problems of a few little people don't amount to a hill of beans - except to them, and their world is our world.
reviews.author: Matt Kelemen

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's delightfully original, bittersweet, slyly campy saga of murder, theft and conspiracy that becomes a whimsical, madcap romp.
reviews.author: Susan Granger

reviews.text: A sublime whodunit designed for cinephiles with sophisticated palates.
reviews.author: Kam Williams

reviews.text: Like the tool-stuffed pastries baked by the film's winsome young Agatha, 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' is an irresistible frosted confection with a steely, purposeful center.
reviews.author: John Beifuss

reviews.text: Just like its namesake, there is something outrageously regal about the movie 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' that makes it a warm and exciting place to check into.
reviews.author: Mathew DeKinder

reviews.text: Like Gene Hackman in The Royal Tenenbaums, Fiennes seems both in sync and immune to Anderson's fastidious nature. It's a tour-de-force performance that should earn an Oscar nomination but will most likely be overlooked in favor of more sober portrayals.
reviews.author: Jeff Meyers

reviews.text: The movie is a flume ride through the imagination of one of the most creative minds making movies today, and the pleasure curls your toes. Also, be ready to crave some macaroons.
reviews.author: Rene Rodriguez

reviews.text: Each part is plum and comedically necessary. Who would have even thought of casting Tilda Swinton or Ralph Fiennes in a wild comedy? Voilà, they seem perfectly cast.
reviews.author: Steve Crum

reviews.text: No film has even come close to matching The Royal Tenenbaums, until now
reviews.author: Kevin Carr

reviews.text: A wondrous celebration of everything that Wes Anderson holds dear - while moving farther away from being a universally recommendable title for casual viewers.
reviews.author: Sandy Schaefer

reviews.text: Wes Anderson checks into a grand hotel
reviews.author: Robert Denerstein

reviews.text: Whrilwind storytelling leaves the emotional core behind
reviews.author: Marty Mapes

reviews.text: You will check in to the Grand Budapest Hotel and find yourself not wanting to leave!
reviews.author: Jolene Mendez

reviews.text: "Budapest" is pretty much an old-fashioned screwball comedy garishly dressed. It's goofy, eccentric and often downright silly. There are many scenes that would have worked in a "Three Stooges" movie.
reviews.author: Tom Long

reviews.text: Budapest Hotel, a vibrant, cheeky throwback to 1930s caper comedies, contains the same high degree of craftsmanship as [Anderson's] other films. There's just more of it.
reviews.author: Carla Meyer

reviews.text: As the actors race, chase and escape across, through and from mansions, mountains and prisons, they bring deadpan theatricality to the old-world artifice and confectionary palette.
reviews.author: Duane Dudek

reviews.text: After feeding on this sweet buffet, sated cinephiles will want to call the front desk to extend their stay.
reviews.author: Joe Williams

reviews.text: When people say, 'They don't make movies like that anymore,' they are wrong. Wes Anderson makes movies like that anymore, and 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' -- part comedy caper, part adventure, and all quirky, embraceable whimsy -- is proof.
reviews.author: Mike Scott

reviews.text: This hotel caper may be Wes Anderson firing on all his quaint idiosyncratic cylinders
reviews.author: Cameron Williams

reviews.text: A brilliant film that is funny, marvelously creative and always just a little bit sad. Easily the best film to come along this year -- and it will probably still be at the end of the year.
reviews.author: Ken Hanke

reviews.text: I'm bothered when an overabundance of surface effects covers up a ringingly hollow purpose, containing very little except authorial will.
reviews.author: Stuart Klawans

reviews.text: In typical Wes Anderson fashion, its impeccable design and je ne sais quoi will win you over.
reviews.author: Cameron Meier

reviews.text: Dense, energetically presented and wonderful - though as my friend suggested, for those first five minutes you'd be forgiven for thinking Anderson was retreading his old tropes a few too many times. Those feelings disappear by the sixth minute.
reviews.author: Patrick Kolan

reviews.text: ...content to operate at an almost infuriating level of consistent quirkiness...
reviews.author: David Nusair

reviews.text: In its own silly, artificial way, it's the first Anderson film to acknowledge the existence of a world outside its own little toy box and to ground its characters' nostalgia in something resembling actual historical reality.
reviews.author: Alex Pappademas

reviews.text: All the cutesiness in the world can't really make what was beginning to happen in 1930s Europe remotely charming, as Anderson seems to want to do.
reviews.author: Richard Lawson

reviews.text: The comedy in The Grand Budapest Hotel is among the broadest yet undertaken by Anderson. But amid the frenzied hubbub, there are intimations of a darker, sadder history unfolding.
reviews.author: Christopher Orr

reviews.text: If a movie can be elegantly zany, this wholly imaginative, assured fable of a legendary concierge Gustave H. (Ralph Fiennes), his protégé Zero (Tony Revolori) and the murder of a countess, is it.
reviews.author: Lisa Kennedy

reviews.text: In The Grand Budapest Hotel, Anderson's eighth feature, the director invests his trademark whimsy with spectacular ambition, and the result is the most richly entertaining film of his career.
reviews.author: Brian D. Johnson

reviews.text: Will charm not only the filmmaker's devoted cult but possibly a few of his detractors.
reviews.author: Kelly Vance

reviews.text: Madcap and exhilarating --- I absolutely loved every minute of "The Grand Budapest Hotel".
reviews.author: Jeanne Kaplan

reviews.text: The late Robert Altman would have loved this film, which practically demands a second viewing.
reviews.author: David Kaplan

reviews.text: Whereas many of Anderson's early films felt a little rough around the edges, The Grand Budapest Hotel - with its shifting aspect ratios, creamy photography, and oh-so-careful 90-degree camera swivels - feels impeccable
reviews.author: Witney Seibold

reviews.text: I was so busy delighting in its breathtaking aesthetic complexity that I suspect the story will work magic on me in later viewings. That's what happened with The Life Aquatic.
reviews.author: Jeffrey Overstreet

reviews.text: The most sophisticated and cosmopolitan comic cinema of our time.
reviews.author: James Verniere

reviews.text: A whimsical, confectionery delight filled with Old World charm and a hint of sadness.
reviews.author: Travis Hopson

reviews.text: It's the movie equivalent of a rich and delicious dessert.
reviews.author: Chris Hewitt

reviews.text: Good, but not the director's best work, it's fun to visit 'The Grand Budapest Hotel.' I just felt it could have been a briefer trip with less highlights and a little more substance. (Content Review for Parents Also Available)
reviews.author: Jim Judy

reviews.text: Imagine a blend of The Muppet Movie, Mel Brooks, and Where's Waldo? and you're halfway to the carnival ride viewing experience Anderson delivers with this gem.
reviews.author: Brian Orndorf

reviews.text: The whole of The Grand Budapest Hotel ... is something entirely different from Anderson, even if the particulars ... are entirely familiar.
reviews.author: Mark Dujsik

reviews.text: From the start, it's clear Anderson is working with a new sophistication both in the vocabulary and structure of the film's voiceover narrations.
reviews.author: Liam Lacey

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is by far the most headlong comedic affair in Anderson's canon. It's practically Marx Brothers-ian at moments. And Fiennes - who knew he was capable of such wicked, witty timing?!
reviews.author: Steven Rea

reviews.text: Fiennes is on fire in one of the best roles of his career.
reviews.author: Willie Waffle

reviews.text: Anderson is the master of "saudade," the nostalgia for something you never had or that never existed.
reviews.author: Nell Minow

reviews.text: It's quintessential Anderson, in other words, but also an unabashed entertainment. And that's something to see.
reviews.author: Bruce Ingram

reviews.text: Anderson's customary lavish production values render the spectacle a visual treat while a quality script maintains decent momentum.
reviews.author: Padraic McKiernan

reviews.text: For all the fancy and fun, this is one of Mr. Anderson's most serious and cerebral films.
reviews.author: Kelly Jane Torrance

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is Wes Anderson's best movie yet, full of whimsy and attention to detail but told in the context of a great fall -- the disappearance of grace and manners in Europe amid the rise of the Nazis.
reviews.author: Charles Ealy

reviews.text: It's clever, and thanks to Fiennes and the inspired production design, it's a whole lot of fun. But it's also flat -- apparently by design.
reviews.author: Katherine Monk

reviews.text: it's Fiennes, under a fairly standard but still formidable stache -- somewhere between a Geraldo and a Selleck -- who is the film's emotional core.
reviews.author: Chris Knight

reviews.text: Playing an Old World charmer with clipped diction and a deliciously foul mouth, Fiennes, making his debut with Anderson's stock company, falls into lockstep with the filmmaker's unmistakable universe.
reviews.author: Chris Vognar

reviews.text: With "The Grand Budapest Hotel," Wes Anderson is up to his old tricks but with a magnanimous new confidence that feels like a gift.
reviews.author: Ty Burr

reviews.text: The entire movie is like a giant, elaborately decorated cake, created by this most exacting of film craftsmen. And how tasty it is!
reviews.author: Peter Howell

reviews.text: A delight to the eye, intricatey designed and flawlessly crafted...[with] a streak of tenderness and melancholy to go along with Anderson's characteristic whimsy and wit.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: it's a caper, and an adventure and a comedy and a sad drama- all of it quintessentially Anderson.
reviews.author: Stephen Silver

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is a marvelous spectacle.
reviews.author: Kimberley Jones

reviews.text: [Anderson's pictures are] comical without actually being funny, inventive without being freely playful, momentous without being dramatic. The emotional oxygen that would ignite them gets smothered in self-conscious cleverness.
reviews.author: Michael Sragow

reviews.text: With this film, Anderson has proven he is one of the greatest American directors working today.
reviews.author: Miriam Bale

reviews.text: Welcome to The Grand Budapest Hotel: An intimate and charming retreat with supreme comfort and guest-themed hospitality.
reviews.author: Chase Whale

reviews.text: The tender friendship between the wide-eyed Zero and the worldly Gustave gives this movie an emotional core that isn't always an Anderson priority.
reviews.author: Rafer Guzman

reviews.text: What follows is a rousing epic, with quintessential Anderson touches (miniatures, quirky camera work, fantastically implausible stunts), and beautiful set design.
reviews.author: Alynda Wheat

reviews.text: I would call "The Grand Budapest Hotel" major whimsy. It's a confection with bite, featuring an ensemble led by the invaluable Ralph Fiennes, here allowed to exercise his farceur's wiles.
reviews.author: Michael Phillips

reviews.text: The movie's sad undertone saves "The Grand Budapest Hotel" from its own zaniness - or better yet, elevates the zaniness, making it feel like an assertion of some right to be silly, or some fundamental human expression.
reviews.author: Mick LaSalle

reviews.text: If Anderson buries relatively little moral substance under lavish dollops of rich cream, at least he, like his fascinating protagonist, sustains the illusion with a marvelous grace.
reviews.author: Ann Hornaday

reviews.text: Anderson shows the value of a filmmaker working at the full, precise capacity of a master chef. The Grand Budapest Hotel is the movie that earns him his third Michelin star.
reviews.author: Matt Pais

reviews.text: Every frame is carefully composed like the illustrations from a beloved book (characters are precisely centered; costumes are elaborately literal); the dialogue feels both unexpected and happily familiar.
reviews.author: Moira MacDonald

reviews.text: Mostly delightful. It can give you the foreboding you feel when encountering the word "artisanal," but otherwise this nested story of Central European skullduggery seems to have more of a spine than anything he's made since Fantastic Mr. Fox.
reviews.author: Richard von Busack

reviews.text: It offers an engaging 90+ minutes of unconventional, comedy-tinged adventure that references numerous classic movies while developing a style and narrative approach all its own.
reviews.author: James Berardinelli

reviews.text: "The Grand Budapest Hotel" shows Anderson engaging with the world outside his meticulously composed frames like never before.
reviews.author: Marc Mohan

reviews.text: You know what to expect when watching one of Anderson's films, and his latest doesn't disappoint, overflowing with colorful characters, zany plot twists and sublime production design.
reviews.author: Jason Zingale

reviews.text: "A comedy about the tragedy of nostalgia..."
reviews.author: Josh Larsen

reviews.text: A sobering message movie that still know hows to tickle us with a goofy ski chase that is joyously and purely Wes Anderson through and through.
reviews.author: Randy Myers

reviews.text: The best film of Anderson's film to date, 'The Grand Budapest Hotel' is amusing and it looks spectacular...
reviews.author: John Esther

reviews.text: It's an infinitely rewatchable treat let down only by what Mary Berry might call the plot's 'soggy middle' involving will disputes and prison breaks.
reviews.author: Larushka Ivan-Zadeh

reviews.text: There is no space in The Grand Budapest Hotel. No vacancy. It is absolutely stuffed with plot points. There is no room to breathe, no room for a joke to settle (or even register) before Anderson has shuttled us off somewhere else.
reviews.author: Brian Formo

reviews.text: A sort of a shaggy-dog story told with manic verve and the narrative dexterity of a meticulously plotted mystery.
reviews.author: Alistair Harkness

reviews.text: The opéra-bouffe plot serves as a strand of bright golden wire on which Anderson hangs innumerable encounters, scampering chases, and an archly decorative style of commentary.
reviews.author: David Denby

reviews.text: Both Anderson's most tightly wound and funniest film in years, lacking the melancholy charm of The Royal Tenenbaums or Moonrise Kingdom perhaps, but more than making up for it in terms of elegantly capering contrivance.
reviews.author: Mark Kermode

reviews.text: I am sure that the cast and crew had a great deal of fun but the finished product is too much of an indulgence to get a place as one of the writer-director's best works.
reviews.author: Robin Clifford

reviews.text: A bravura chunk of pastiche.
reviews.author: Ed Whitfield

reviews.text: This beautiful film is at its best when it so delicately underscores one of its major ideas, that of learning to let go of a past - a romantic way of life, a virtuous belief system, genteel traditions and rituals - in order to move on with the present.
reviews.author: Tina Hassannia

reviews.text: It's a time capsule, showing us the twilight of a man and his era, subverting rosy nostalgic currents to memorialize life's fleeting shadow.
reviews.author: Robert Levin

reviews.text: Set in a deluxe spa hotel occupying an imaginary corner of Mitteleuropa between the wars, Wes Anderson's new film pampers the viewer with its sumptuous visual delights, sparkling dialogue and absurdly enjoyable comic intrigue.
reviews.author: Jason Best

reviews.text: A vivid, multilayered story of history and fantasy, fiction and emotional truth, which only falters when it ventures too close to events whose harrowing reality probably shouldn't be reduced to a quirky backdrop for the filmmaker's twee melodramas.
reviews.author: Todd Gilchrist

reviews.text: An Anderson confection is always a visual and aural delight.
reviews.author: Annlee Ellingson

reviews.text: ...a fitfully amusing cuckoo clockworks, but although its nostalgic yearnings for the craftsmanship of yesterday, a Sehnsucht, is palpable, it lacks the real heart found in Anderson's better works.
reviews.author: Laura Clifford

reviews.text: Witty, whimsical farce with some cartoonish violence.
reviews.author: S. Jhoanna Robledo

reviews.text: It's Fiennes who coolly walks off with the film. Switching seamlessly between courtliness and profanity, he displays a gift for comic timing that's rarely been unleashed since his Essex gang boss in 2007's In Bruges.
reviews.author: Philip Kemp

reviews.text: What smothers the comedy is the palpable effort that goes into each set piece or joke. The whimsical tone grows wearisome when the gags fall flat.
reviews.author: Ryan Gilbey

reviews.text: Against the backdrop of a new locale, as well as a mosaic of cameos that move the plot forward through each new farcical twist, the film achieves a wonderful rhythm in which we're delighted to expect the unexpected, and sometimes we're still surprised.
reviews.author: Cammila Collar

reviews.text: Add in the director's gift for nesting stories, his taste for grotesques and his exquisite eye, and you have the best Wes Anderson film in a decade
reviews.author: Donald Clarke

reviews.text: A higgledy-piggledy tutti-frutti concoction that also has its share of old-world melancholy.
reviews.author: Peter Rainer

reviews.text: What's special about this film is that, while it bears all the hallmarks of his by-now entirely too familiar style, it also finds him acknowledging the limitations of that style when it butts up against a certain measure of reality
reviews.author: Ethan Alter

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel is not so much a movie as ordinarily understood as a Wunderkammer or cabinet of curiosities.
reviews.author: David Sexton

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's entertaining filmmaking style clicks beautifully into focus for this comical adventure.
reviews.author: Rich Cline

reviews.text: A clockwork wedding cake, a caper movie sprinkled with pixie dust, a picture that sends you scrambling for clever metaphors and failing to find them.
reviews.author: Kurt Loder

reviews.text: To answer some folks who claim to enjoy Anderson's movies while also grousing that they wish he would apply his cinematic talents in a "different" mode: no, this isn't the movie in which he does what you think you want, whatever that is.
reviews.author: Glenn Kenny

reviews.text: This is one of Anderson's funniest and most fanciful movies, but perversely enough it may also be his most serious, most tragic and most shadowed by history, with the frothy Ernst Lubitsch-style comedy shot through with an overwhelming sense of loss.
reviews.author: Andrew O'Hehir

reviews.text: With comic timing like this, Fiennes is wasted on Shakespeare.
reviews.author: Andy Lea

reviews.text: Director Wes Anderson's films are so artistically exquisite that they should be framed and mounted. And this effort may be his most astounding.
reviews.author: Mara Reinstein

reviews.text: Gorgeous, whimsical and wonderfully imaginative, The Grand Budapest Hotel is a dazzling piece of eye candy with a deceptively emotional center - in other words, it's Anderson's most ambitious and impressive film to date.
reviews.author: Isaac Feldberg

reviews.text: It is a gorgeous film to look at.
reviews.author: Brian Viner

reviews.text: Grand Budapest is a culmination of the tinkly music-box aesthetic of Anderson's work to date, turned up to 11.
reviews.author: Ian Buckwalter

reviews.text: It's a mature, intricately layered visual delight.
reviews.author: Claudia Puig

reviews.text: [The Grand Budapest Hotel] makes the best possible argument in favor of artistic fussiness, packing layers of allusions, characters, jokes, plot turns, and emotion into a film that carries itself with the lightness of a soufflé.
reviews.author: Scott Tobias

reviews.text: Anderson works so assiduously to create obsessively detailed on-screen worlds that the effect has sometimes been hermetic, even stifling. "The Grand Budapest," however, is anything but.
reviews.author: Kenneth Turan

reviews.text: In Anderson's hands, the revolution is ridiculous, and that buys him room to grapple with some big ideas at the same time in what I am sure is one of the best films he's made to date.
reviews.author: Drew McWeeny

reviews.text: It's a filigreed toy box of a movie, so delicious-looking you may want to lick the screen. It is also, in the Anderson manner, shot through with humor, heartbreak and a bruised romantic's view of the past.
reviews.author: Peter Travers

reviews.text: Mr. Anderson's lovely confection ... keeps us smiling, and sometimes laughing out loud. Yet acid lurks in the cake's lowest layers.
reviews.author: Joe Morgenstern

reviews.text: The ornamental riches queue up: production design, star cast, pastiche stylings of gesture, costume, dialogue in a story set in Belle Époque Central Europe. But not a sustaining calorie, narrative or dramatic, in sight.
reviews.author: Nigel Andrews

reviews.text: Watched once, it's the most entertaining movie in theaters. Revisited, it's the saddest.
reviews.author: Matt Prigge

reviews.text: As with all of Anderson's films, the magic is in the cast. Fiennes, with his rapid-fire delivery and rapier mustache, is hilarious, dapper and total perfection.
reviews.author: Joe Neumaier

reviews.text: There are hints that Fiennes has it in him to portray a worthwhile human being here -- tender, smart, impulsive, humane, and witty -- but this potential is smothered by Anderson's chronic preference for guest stars and demented art direction.
reviews.author: David Thomson

reviews.text: Divine pastries, divine clothes, divine period trappings, but, as with most of Anderson's films, I was never moved or understood what mattered, if any of it mattered. I'm even forgetting it as I'm remembering it, as if it had been no more than a dream.
reviews.author: Deborah Ross

reviews.text: True enchantment will elude those, like me, who remain impervious to Anderson's affected style and whimsical humour.
reviews.author: Henry Fitzherbert

reviews.text: An absolute treat from start to finish ...
reviews.author: Matthew Turner

reviews.text: Time to check out (or into) The Grand Budapest Hotel.
reviews.author: Tim Evans

reviews.text: A deeply pleasurable immersion.
reviews.author: Peter Bradshaw

reviews.text: This movie makes a marvelous mockery of history, turning its horrors into a series of graceful jokes and mischievous gestures. You can call this escapism if you like. You can also think of it as revenge.
reviews.author: A.O. Scott

reviews.text: Imaginative, charming and wonderfully funny. It's sure to become one of Anderson's most beloved narratives.
reviews.author: Kristy Puchko

reviews.text: Anderson has made a madcap caper that doubles as a winsome eulogy for such archaic virtues as glamour, civility, and dutiful customer service.
reviews.author: A.A. Dowd

reviews.text: Presented like a Tintin comic strip with just a hint of early Hitchcock.
reviews.author: William Bibbiani

reviews.text: For once, Anderson will let his airless snow globe be shaken and dropped, and in this case crudely glued back together by Communism, coyly referred to as the time of "common property"
reviews.author: Amy Nicholson

reviews.text: In the end it's Fiennes who makes the biggest impression. His stylized, rapid-fire delivery, dry wit and cheerful profanity keep the movie bubbling along. Here's to further Fiennes-Anderson collaborations.
reviews.author: Jocelyn Noveck

reviews.text: [It] feels like Wes Anderson's most heartfelt film thus far. One that effortlessly straddles genres and works as both a nostalgic paean to a more innocent time and an examination of the very nature of storytelling itself.
reviews.author: Chris Tilly

reviews.text: We're used to a Wes Anderson movie charming us. Get ready for one that's downright thrilling.
reviews.author: Tim Grierson

reviews.text: I amaze myself by liking this latest lunatic cocktail as much as I do.
reviews.author: Rex Reed

reviews.text: I've had my Wes Anderson breakthrough - or maybe it's that he's had his. The Grand Budapest Hotel is a marvelous contraption, a wheels-within-wheels thriller that's pure oxygenated movie play.
reviews.author: Owen Gleiberman

reviews.text: It is the deft, exceptionally light touch that Fiennes brings to moments both comic and serious that gives this engine its fuel.
reviews.author: Marshall Fine

reviews.text: The auteur's style-dramatic zooms, winking symmetry-is balanced against a newfound political context; this one's his To Be or Not to Be.
reviews.author: Joshua Rothkopf

reviews.text: Europe is just this nutty place where a lot of crazy mixed-up stuff happened and look at this darling model ski lift! That's Wes Anderson: He can't see the forest for the twee.
reviews.author: Kyle Smith

reviews.text: A madcap, inventive, and wonder-inducing creation about the arts of living from the inimitable writer and director Wes Anderson.
reviews.author: Frederic and Mary Ann Brussat

reviews.text: Wes Anderson delivers a luxury film experience in the shape of The Grand Budapest Hotel, a feast for the eyes with a ritzy, glitzy cast and touches of comedy gold courtesy of Ralph Fiennes.
reviews.author: Stella Papamichael

reviews.text: Every shot is gorgeously framed, with screwball rhythms patterned after 1930s European ironists such as Ernst Lubitsch and Billy Wilder.
reviews.author: Siobhan Synnot

reviews.text: Another meticulously stylish and deadpan Wes Anderson movie that walks the fine line between masterpiece and folly.
reviews.author: Damon Wise

reviews.text: It's fitting that a recurring piece of pastry plays a role in the story, since Wes Anderson seems to be daring us to view his work as mere confection, while offering subtle evidence that there's more at play.
reviews.author: Jesse Cataldo

reviews.text: Behind the predictably whimsical yarn of a hotel concierge on the run lies a darker tale of pre-war Europe, a land of intrigue, disease, love and bubbling violence.
reviews.author: Sam Lewis

reviews.text: A movie that, for all its gorgeous frills and furbelows ... never seemed to me to be quite sure what it was about.
reviews.author: Dana Stevens

reviews.text: An exquisitely calibrated, deadpan-comic miniature that expands in the mind and becomes richer and more tragic.
reviews.author: David Edelstein

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's eighth film dazzles and delights as if it has been liberated from the pages of a beautifully illustrated storybook.
reviews.author: Emma Simmonds

reviews.text: A memory of a memory, a fastidious, whimsical take on real horrors - a storybook samizdat that entices with madcap adventure then goes in for the kill with existential dread.
reviews.author: Jordan Hoffman

reviews.text: It's his grandest plaything to date, his most splendid and glittering toy -- yet for all the ornamentation on display, it's also his most human and humane.
reviews.author: Shane Danielsen

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's post-Fantastic Mr Fox whimsy hits its stride as storybook style meets thematic substance in this gorgeous, joyful, yet far from featherlight end-of-an-era yarn.
reviews.author: Michael Leader

reviews.text: Anderson has conquered scale and story, balancing humor and deep emotion. His antic period piece about a "liberally perfumed" concierge of a once-grand Eastern European resort (Ralph Fiennes), is charming, wondrous, nostalgic and dazzlingly original.
reviews.author: Thelma Adams

reviews.text: [Wes Anderson's] new film, The Grand Budapest Hotel, ranks among his best, an ambitious and highly original concoction featuring an irresistible lead performance by Ralph Fiennes.
reviews.author: Kevin Lally

reviews.text: Lush and gorgeous and colorful and twee and utterly obviously fake.
reviews.author: Anne Thompson

reviews.text: Like the eye-catching cakes Agatha makes, Wes Anderson's eighth feature has a heft beneath its icing, heart behind its artifice. Check in, and you won't want to leave.
reviews.author: Emma Morgan

reviews.text: No amount of visual invention can substitute for characters, though, and Anderson doesn't so much write characters anymore as recruit a great cast and dress them up.
reviews.author: J. R. Jones

reviews.text: Wes Anderson is the Willy Wonka of art films. He works in a land of pure imagination. You never know what will be around the next corner. But you do have a sense of what the chocolate will taste like.
reviews.author: David Poland

reviews.text: The film's shaggy-dog, sort-of-whodunit yarn offers laughs and energy that make this Anderson's most fun film since Rushmore.
reviews.author: Dave Calhoun

reviews.text: An opulent and strangely moving caper movie.
reviews.author: David Jenkins

reviews.text: [The Grand Budapest Hotel] might just be the most Wes Anderson-y film yet made by Wes Anderson.
reviews.author: Francesca Steele

reviews.text: It's Anderson's darkest work yet - and, despite its far-off setting, one of his most hauntingly personal.
reviews.author: Jon Frosch

reviews.text: The downside of incredibly choreographed, ornately patterned, sumptuously appointed music box scenes is that they tend to render the characters as sexless wooden figurines.
reviews.author: Vincent Mancini

reviews.text: Even those of us who genuinely look forward to the cinematic adventure that is each and every Wes Anderson film can be disappointed.
reviews.author: Kirk Honeycutt

reviews.text: Not only does Anderson create a country here, he creates a parallel, but slightly crazy-mirror version of history too, all delivered through the prism of Golden Age Hollywood comedies-we truly cannot fault his ambition.
reviews.author: Jessica Kiang

reviews.text: A little real human feeling and a lot of real-world filming would do more for both Anderson's career and audience than yet another of his seemingly endless, seemingly fruitless clockwork comedic contraptions
reviews.author: James Rocchi

reviews.text: It's in Ralph Fiennes's performance as M. Gustave, his Andersonian affectless ruptured by real pathos and frustration, that The Grand Budapest grounds itself.
reviews.author: John Semley

reviews.text: It's a typical Anderson film, flourishing in a world of its own, which Fiennes inhabits and oversees to the manor born.
reviews.author: Derek Malcolm

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's ingenious and imaginative The Grand Budapest Hotel beautifully delivers 100 minutes of pure delight.
reviews.author: Anna Tatarska

reviews.text: Over the years, Wes Anderson's movies have steadily developed a lush, eccentric world that operates on its own terms, and "The Grand Budapest Hotel" excels at exploring it.
reviews.author: Eric Kohn

reviews.text: Anderson has hit on the ideal narrative context for his restless romanticism and production design fetish.
reviews.author: Guy Lodge

reviews.text: This is the moment in the Anderson oeuvre when he turns to consider all things Mitteleuropäische - refracted, as a closing credit tells us, through the work of the prolific Austrian writer Stefan Zweig.
reviews.author: Andrew Pulver

reviews.text: In a very appealing if outre way, its sensibility and concerns are very much those of an earlier, more elegant era, meaning that the film's deepest intentions will fly far over the heads of most modern filmgoers.
reviews.author: Todd McCarthy

reviews.text: Anderson has created a whimsical, dreamlike world where anything goes, allowing him the licence to do whatever he sees fit. So by all means indulge in GBH - the sort that won't land you in jail.
reviews.author: Stefan Pape

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's captivating 1930s-set caper offers a vibrant and imaginative evocation of a bygone era.
reviews.author: Justin Chang

reviews.text: Wes Anderson's beautiful and thoroughly enjoyable The Grand Budapest Hotel sees the director deliver his best film.
reviews.author: Mark Adams

reviews.text: You might get light-headed on the pure fun of it, which unleashes fresh waves of fun-within-fun at every point where you worry it could dry up.
reviews.author: Tim Robey

reviews.text: The Grand Budapest Hotel brought out my inner Hunca Munca, of Two Bad Mice fame: This meticulously appointed dollhouse of a movie just went on and on, making me want to smash many miniature plates of plaster food in frustration.
reviews.author: Stephanie Zacharek

reviews.text: Course after course of desserts, presented with a flourish and served so promptly that you can barely catch your breath between treats. It's not until an hour or two has passed that you realize that you haven't really eaten anything.
reviews.author: Alonso Duralde

reviews.text: Truly one of [Wes Anderson's] most inspired films, as much influenced by classic cinemas as it maintains his own sense of style and pace.
reviews.author: Edward Douglas

synopsis: In the 1930s, the Grand Budapest Hotel is a popular European ski resort, presided over by concierge Gustave H. (Ralph Fiennes). Zero, a junior lobby boy, becomes Gustave's friend and protege. Gustave prides himself on providing first-class service to the hotel's guests, including satisfying the sexual needs of the many elderly women who stay there. When one of Gustave's lovers dies mysteriously, Gustave finds himself the recipient of a priceless painting and the chief suspect in her murder.
